newsitem.title: USA: Search goes on for missing Air Force plane.
newsitem.headline: Search goes on for missing Air Force plane.

text.p: Rescue workers looking for an A-10 warplane that disappeared 10 days ago have expanded their search in rugged, mountainous terrain to five areas from two, military officials said on Saturday.
"I am optimistic that we're getting information in those areas," Lt.-Gen. Frank Campbell of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base told a news briefing in Eagle, Colorado.
Campbell said a U-2 spy plane that flew over the area in western Colorado was sending information to computers in California to be analysed.

He said photo interpreters analysing information from prior flights led officials to add three areas to their search list. But he said it was too early to send ground troops into any of the areas where the missing plane, loaded with four bombs, may have gone down.
Heavy snow and cold temperatures have restricted rescue efforts, leaving officials to hope radar information will help them find the aircraft.
Campbell said the Air Force was not operating under any assumptions about whether the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, was alive or had perished in a crash.
"We're simply following the evidence as we have it," he said. "We don't have evidence that he is alive, and we don't have evidence that he isn't alive."
But the disappearance of the plane has turned into a mystery, prompting speculation the plane may have been stolen.
Officials have said they have no evidence of that, but said they have been going over Button's background as well as what he did in the days before the April 2 training exercise.

Rescue workers are hoping to at least find an engine or an engine part from the A-10. "Normally what survives a crash, not intact, certainly damaged, but recognisable as a piece of an airplane is normally an engine," Campbell said. "A lot of times the rest of the aircraft is not really recognisable."
The tank-attacking A-10 Thunderbolt piloted by Button disappeared after it left Davis-Monthan Air Force base in Tucson, Arizona, during a routine training exercise in southwest Arizona.
Defence officials said the plane, carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) conventional Mark 82 bombs, disappeared from the rear of a three-plane formation.

A week ago officials announced the search had been expanded to Colorado after radar tracking data indicated the plane may have flown to a location about 15 miles (25 km) southwest of the Vail ski resort.
Eyewitness accounts have also suggested the plane may have crashed in that area. Air Force officials said they do not know why Button left the formation during the exercise.
